title: Wounded Hope: Narrative Identity, Vulnerability, and Forgiveness in Religious Education
content: Contemporary religious education encounters young people whose identities are formed amid vulnerability, social fragmentation, moral plurality, and digitally mediated narratives of self and world. This conceptual article develops wounded hope as a distinctive hermeneutical and pedagogical construct for religious education (RE). Wounded hope names an orientation that holds truthful memory of irreversible harm together with an ethically open future in which neither identity nor agency is exhausted by the wound. Paul Ricoeur supplies the principal hermeneutical architecture through narrative identity, mimesis, memory, recognition, and refiguration. Gabriel Marcel, Jürgen Moltmann, Paulo Freire, and Thomas Groome deepen and correct that architecture through philosophical hope, eschatological contradiction, critical praxis, and shared Christian praxis. Recent scholarship on Ricoeur, vulnerability, trauma-responsive education, youth flourishing, church-school climate, and digital religion is brought into dialogue with these foundational sources. The article argues that wounded hope is not optimism, resilience, post-traumatic growth, or a theology of redemptive suffering. It further contends that forgiveness in RE must remain a religious and ethical possibility rather than a compulsory educational outcome, and must be distinguished from forgetting, excusing, reconciliation, restored trust, and the suspension of justice. Developed from within a Catholic-Christian horizon while remaining dialogically open to wider RE, the article proposes a Narrative Pedagogy of Wounded Hope structured by five commitments: narrative hospitality, hermeneutical dialogue, critical discernment, hopeful refiguration, and ethical agency. Reflexively, the proposal also examines its own risks: theological overreach, therapeutic colonisation of education, the privileging of coherence, and the temptation to make hope itself coercive. Wounded hope is therefore offered not as a technique for repairing learners but as a disciplined educational disposition for inhabiting unfinished stories truthfully, critically, and hopefully.
